chapters.customSummary:
- The client (GUI or CLI) is a lens on the database with its own settings and quirks, easily mistaken for database behavior.
- Confirm connection identity (DATABASE(), host, user, version) before running anything unfamiliar; use unmistakable, color-coded connection names, especially to mark production.
- Check and control autocommit/transaction mode in the client's UI (DBeaver/Workbench toggle, psql/mysql CLI defaults) before writes on shared databases.
- Distinguish "run current statement" from "run whole script" shortcuts; run one statement at a time when experimenting on shared data.
- Result grids apply their own formatting: row-count caps with silent pagination, text truncation, inconsistent NULL-vs-empty rendering, date/numeric display rounding — verify anything suspicious with an explicit query (HEX, LENGTH, CAST), never trust the rendered cell.
- Inline grid editing generates UPDATEs that may key off all visible columns, not just the PK, risking unintended matches; prefer explicit UPDATE ... WHERE statements for anything that matters.
- Autocomplete/schema caches go stale after migrations; refresh before trusting what autocomplete implies, and verify structure with information_schema/SHOW CREATE TABLE instead.
- Multi-statement runs can produce several result tabs; check every tab, not just the first, for silent errors or unexpected rows.
- Learn format/beautify, comment-toggle, and explain-plan shortcuts.
- CLI clients (mysql, psql, sqlcmd) have no safety net by default; use --safe-updates/sql_safe_updates, \set ON_ERROR_STOP on, and read scripts fully before piping them in.
- Match client to task: GUI for exploration/diagrams, CLI for scripted/CI work, a cross-dialect tool when working across databases.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## The client is not the database
Everything in this manual has been the SQL itself. This chapter is about the program you type it into: a GUI tool (DBeaver, MySQL Workbench, pgAdmin, Azure Data Studio, TablePlus), a command-line shell (mysql, psql, sqlcmd), or an IDE plugin (JetBrains' database tool, VS Code extensions). The client is a lens on the database, and it has its own settings, quirks and failure modes that are easy to mistake for database behaviour. A tester who understands the client avoids a whole category of false alarms.
## Connecting: know exactly what you're pointed at
Every connection profile has a host, port, database/schema, user and (often) a default character set and time zone. Before running anything on an unfamiliar or shared connection, confirm where you actually are:
```sql
SELECT DATABASE() AS db, @@hostname AS host, @@port AS port, CURRENT_USER() AS you, @@version AS version;
-- PostgreSQL: SELECT current_database(), inet_server_addr(), inet_server_port(), current_user, version();
-- SQL Server: SELECT DB_NAME(), @@SERVERNAME, SYSTEM_USER, @@VERSION;
```

Save connection profiles with unmistakable names and colours ("QA — safe", "STAGING — careful", "PROD — read-only, ask first") rather than generic labels like "MySQL 1" and "MySQL 2." Most GUI clients let you colour-code a connection's tab or toolbar; use production red and never let it look like anything else. The single most common way testers cause real damage is running a script against the wrong tab because two connections looked identical.
## Autocommit and transaction mode, in the client's own UI
0.4 and 7.3 covered the concept; here's where to check and change it in practice. DBeaver shows an "Auto-commit" toggle in the SQL editor toolbar (a green checkmark icon) and lets you switch to manual commit per connection. MySQL Workbench has the same toggle in the results grid toolbar. psql defaults to autocommit-per-statement unless you type BEGIN; mysql CLI is autocommit by default (\c doesn't change it — use SET autocommit=0 or START TRANSACTION). Before any UPDATE/DELETE on a shared database, glance at that toggle. If manual-commit mode is on and you forget to commit or roll back, you can leave a transaction open and block other sessions for the rest of your coffee break (7.3's "hung QA environment" story).
## Query execution: run one statement, not the whole script
GUI editors typically bind two different shortcuts: "execute the statement under the cursor" and "execute the whole script/file." It's easy to hit the wrong one and run every DELETE in a scratch file at once. Get comfortable with your client's statement-boundary shortcut (often Ctrl+Enter / Cmd+Enter for "current statement" versus Ctrl+Shift+Enter / a toolbar "execute script" button for "everything"), and prefer running one statement at a time when experimenting on a shared database, even inside a transaction.
## Result grids: what you see is not always what's stored
Client grids apply their own formatting and truncation, and treating the grid's display as ground truth causes false bug reports:
Row limits. Many GUI tools cap the visible result set (DBeaver defaults to a "fetch size" and a max rows setting, often 200), silently paginating with a "Fetch more" link at the bottom. A COUNT(*) you never ran can look like "only 200 rows exist" if you just scroll the grid and stop.
Column truncation. Long text and TEXT/BLOB columns are often shown abbreviated with an ellipsis, or as (BLOB)/<binary> placeholders. A trailing space or an invisible character (2.5) is invisible in a truncated cell.
NULL vs empty string rendering. Some clients show both as a blank cell, some show NULL in italics or grey, some show <null> literally. Confirm your client's convention before concluding a column "has no value" — DBeaver, for instance, is configurable on this point, and the default can differ between its SQL editor grid and its data editor grid.
Date/time display and rounding. A client may apply its own locale formatting or truncate seconds/microseconds on screen while the stored value is more precise; don't diagnose a "the time is wrong" bug from the grid alone — re-query with explicit formatting (DATE_FORMAT, TO_CHAR) to see the raw stored value.
Numeric display. A grid may show 57500 for a DECIMAL(10,2) value of 57500.00, hiding trailing zero precision that might matter for a rounding investigation (2.4).
When something in a grid looks suspicious, the fix is always the same: query for it explicitly (SELECT HEX(col), SELECT LENGTH(col), SELECT CAST(col AS CHAR)) rather than trusting the rendered cell, exactly the technique 2.5 used to unmask invisible whitespace.
## Editing data directly in a grid
Most GUI clients let you double-click a cell and edit it, generating an UPDATE behind the scenes when you commit the change. This is convenient and dangerous in equal measure: it's easy to fat-finger an edit into the wrong row (especially in an unsorted or unfiltered grid where row order isn't guaranteed, 2.2), and some tools generate the UPDATE's WHERE clause from all visible columns rather than the primary key, which can silently match and update more rows than you intended if the "identifying" columns aren't actually unique. Prefer writing an explicit UPDATE ... WHERE id = ... statement over inline grid editing whenever the change matters, precisely so you control the WHERE clause yourself (0.4's safe-workflow habit).
## Autocomplete and object caches
GUI clients cache the list of tables/columns for autocomplete, and that cache can go stale after a schema migration (6.4) — autocomplete still offering a dropped column, or not yet offering a newly added one, is a client artifact, not evidence the migration failed. Refresh the schema cache (usually F5 or a right-click "Refresh") before trusting what autocomplete implies about current structure, and always verify structural questions with an actual information_schema query or SHOW CREATE TABLE, not the autocomplete list.
## Multiple result sets and multi-statement scripts
Running several SELECTs (or a stored procedure that returns more than one result set, 8.3) in one execution produces several grids or tabs. It's easy to look at only the first and miss that a later statement returned unexpected rows, or errored silently while the client moved on. Check whether your client shows a per-statement status/error indicator, and get in the habit of scrolling through every result tab, not just the first, after a multi-statement run.
## Keyboard shortcuts worth learning
Beyond "execute statement" vs "execute script," the shortcuts that save the most time are: format/beautify SQL (turns a one-line paste into readable indentation, useful when a developer pastes a query in Slack), comment/uncomment a line or block (for toggling a WHERE clause on and off while debugging a query, as 2.1 recommended), and "explain plan" (often bound directly, skipping the need to type EXPLAIN by hand, 8.5). Different clients bind these differently; five minutes with your specific tool's shortcut cheat sheet pays for itself within the first debugging session.
## Command-line clients: no safety net by default
The mysql, psql and sqlcmd CLIs have no grid, no autocomplete cache, and (by default) no confirmation prompts — they execute exactly what you type, and pressing Enter after a DELETE FROM employees with no WHERE runs it immediately. Their advantage is scriptability (exactly what 6.4's clone/restore commands and 7.5's batch loads rely on) and that they're always available over SSH when a GUI tool isn't. A few defensive habits: MySQL's --safe-updates (or -U) flag refuses UPDATE/DELETE without a WHERE or LIMIT (the CLI equivalent of sql_safe_updates, 0.4); psql's \set ON_ERROR_STOP on halts a script on the first error instead of plowing through the rest, which matters when a multi-statement script partially fails (6.4's half-migrated-database scenario); and piping a script through less or cat to read it fully before piping it into the client (mysql < script.sql) is worth the extra ten seconds every time, especially for a script someone else handed you.

| Choosing a client for the task | Task | Good fit | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ad hoc exploration, autocomplete, ER diagrams | GUI (DBeaver, Workbench, pgAdmin) | Visual schema browsing (8.6), grid editing for quick checks | Scripted/repeatable runs, CI, automation |
| CLI (mysql, psql) | Scriptable, no GUI dependency, works over SSH | Cross-dialect work (MySQL one day, PostgreSQL the next) | DBeaver or Azure Data Studio |
| One tool, consistent shortcuts, across many dialects | Reviewing a colleague's query before running it | Any editor with syntax highlighting, read it before connecting | Catches an obviously missing WHERE before execution |

chapters.customSummary:
- A read replica continuously receives primary writes but accepts only reads; it enforces read-only at the infrastructure level, stronger than an account-level restriction alone.
- Check replica status/lag (SHOW REPLICA STATUS, pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp) before relying on freshness.
- Replication lag causes a specific flakiness pattern: write via API (hits primary), immediately read from replica, row isn't there yet — not a race in the app, a race in test infrastructure.
- Fix: verify immediately-after-write assertions against the primary; reserve replica reads for staleness-tolerant checks; if only replica access exists, poll with a bounded timeout rather than an arbitrary sleep().
- Choosing an environment for a task is a checklist against 0.4's ladder: needs writes → writable sandbox, never a replica or production; needs production-scale volume → sized staging clone or a read replica for read-only perf; needs exact current production data → production replica if policy allows; destructive/exploratory → disposable clone; fast/disposable for CI → ephemeral per-run database.
- Layer session-level read-only protection (SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY) even on a replica, as defense in depth against misconfiguration.
- Backups matter to testers too: an unrestored backup is unverified; point-in-time recovery helps investigate historical data state for anomalies.
chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Why "safe" needs its own chapter
0.4 established environments (Dev/QA/Staging/Prod) and access levels in general terms. This chapter goes one level deeper into a specific, very common setup: read replicas, and the broader question of which environment a given testing task should actually run against.
## What a read replica is
A read replica is a copy of a database that continuously receives changes from a primary (the database the application writes to) but only accepts read (SELECT) queries itself. Applications and reporting tools are often pointed at a replica for read-heavy work, to keep that load off the primary, and testers are frequently given replica access specifically because it's structurally impossible to write to it — a stronger guarantee than "please don't write" on a regular QA database (0.5's principle of least privilege, applied at the infrastructure level rather than just the account level).
-- MySQL: is this connection a replica, and how far behind is it?
```sql
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G           -- (MySQL 8.0.22+; older versions: SHOW SLAVE STATUS)
-- key fields: Replica_IO_Running, Replica_SQL_Running, Seconds_Behind_Source
```

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: check replication lag
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replication_lag;
```

## Replication lag is a real testing hazard, not just an infrastructure concern
A replica is not instantaneous. There's always some delay (often milliseconds, sometimes much longer under load) between a write landing on the primary and that same write appearing on the replica. This directly causes a specific, confusing class of test flakiness already flagged in passing back in 7.7: write through the API (which hits the primary), then immediately read from the replica to verify, and the row isn't there yet — not because the write failed, but because it hasn't replicated. The test fails intermittently, passes on retry, and looks exactly like a race condition in the application when it's actually a race condition in your test infrastructure.
```py
def test_created_employee_is_readable(replica_db, api_base_url):
    resp = requests.post(f"{api_base_url}/employees", json={...})
    employee_id = resp.json()["id"]
```

## # WRONG: may flake under replication lag
    replica_db.execute("SELECT * FROM employees WHERE employee_id = %s", (employee_id,))
## assert replica_db.fetchone() is not None

## # BETTER: poll with a bounded timeout, or read from the primary for verification
## # immediately after a write, and only use the replica for checks that can tolerate
## # being slightly stale (dashboards, reports, anything not asserting "just happened")

The fix, in order of preference: verify immediately-after-write assertions against the primary, not the replica, and reserve replica reads for checks where staleness genuinely doesn't matter (a report that's allowed to be "as of a few seconds ago"); or, if only replica access is available, poll with a bounded retry loop rather than asserting immediately, exactly the pattern used for asynchronous job completion elsewhere in this manual (7.7's "wait for async jobs to finish" point from 6.6 applies identically here). Never paper over this by adding an arbitrary sleep() before the assertion — that either makes tests slower than necessary on a fast day or still flaky on a slow one; a poll-with-timeout is the correct shape.
## Choosing the right environment for the task, revisited
0.4 laid out the general Dev/QA/Staging/Production ladder. In practice, the choice for a specific testing task usually comes down to a short list of questions:
Question
Points toward
## Does this need to write data?
A writable environment (QA, or a dedicated sandbox) — never a read replica, never (in normal circumstances) production
## Does this need production-scale volume for a performance test (8.5, 7.5)?
A staging clone sized like production, or a read replica of production itself if read-only performance is what's being measured
Does this need to match production's exact current data for a specific investigation (an anomaly hunt, 10.1)?
A production read replica, if policy allows, since QA/staging data may be masked (7.6) or simply different
Is this a destructive or exploratory test (constraint-breaking, migration testing, 6.4, 8.1)?
A disposable clone, never anything shared
Does this need to be fast and disposable for CI (9.4)?
## An ephemeral per-run database

The recurring theme, consistent with everything from 0.4 onward: match the environment's properties (writable or not, shared or not, real-scale or not, real data or masked) to what the specific test genuinely needs, rather than defaulting to whichever connection happens to be open in your client.
## Read-only enforcement: defense in depth
A read replica enforces read-only at the infrastructure level, but it's worth layering additional protection even there, because a misconfigured replica occasionally does accept writes, and "the replica should be read-only" is itself sometimes exactly the thing you're testing (a failed failover, a replica accidentally promoted). The session-level protections from 10.2's sanity-runner safety section apply just as well here:
```sql
SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY;         -- MySQL: any write attempt in this session now errors immediately
-- PostgreSQL: SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
```

Running this at the start of any exploratory session on a replica (or any environment where you want a hard guarantee against accidental writes) costs nothing and catches a class of "I typed UPDATE on the wrong tab" mistake before it can do damage — a second line of defense behind the account-level read-only permission from 0.5.
## Backups and restores as a testing concern
Backups aren't purely a DBA topic; testers rely on restores constantly (cloning for migration testing in 6.4, refreshing a stale staging environment, recovering after a destructive test went wrong on a database that shouldn't have been shared but was). Two things worth knowing at a tester's level of depth, without needing to run the tooling yourself:
A backup that's never been restored is unverified. The only proof a backup actually works is successfully restoring it. If your team's disaster-recovery process has never been tested end to end, that's worth flagging as a gap, the same way an untested rollback script was flagged as a gap in 6.4.
Point-in-time recovery (restoring to a specific moment, not just the latest full backup) matters for investigating "what did the data look like right before this bug happened" — useful when an anomaly (10.1) needs historical context that a live query can no longer provide because the bad data has since been fixed or overwritten.

chapters.title: 11.3 Exporting Query Results for Bug Reports
chapters.overviewText: Every chapter from 4.3 onward has ended defect-hunting queries with some version of "attach this as evidence." This chapter is the mechanics: how to actually get a query result out of the database and into a bug tracker, a chat message, or a shared document, in a form the reader can use without re-running anything themselves. chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Evidence needs to survive outside the SQL client
Every chapter from 4.3 onward has ended defect-hunting queries with some version of "attach this as evidence." This chapter is the mechanics: how to actually get a query result out of the database and into a bug tracker, a chat message, or a shared document, in a form the reader can use without re-running anything themselves.
## What makes exported evidence useful versus useless
A screenshot of a result grid, cropped to fit, with the query nowhere in sight, is close to useless: the reader can't verify it, can't re-run it after a fix, and often can't even tell which environment it came from. Useful evidence consistently includes four things: the exact query that produced it (so it's reproducible), the environment and timestamp it was run against (so staleness is visible, 6.5's drift concerns apply to evidence too), the full relevant result (not a cropped screenshot missing rows), and enough surrounding context (row counts, what an empty result would have meant) that the reader doesn't have to guess what "success" would have looked like.
## CSV export: the default for tabular evidence
Every client supports exporting a result grid to CSV, and it's the right default for anything the reader might want to filter, sort, or paste into a spreadsheet themselves.
```sql
-- MySQL: server-side export (writes to the DB server's filesystem, needs FILE privilege)
SELECT employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, allowances, deductions, net_pay
FROM payroll WHERE pay_month = '2026-08-01'
```
## INTO OUTFILE '/tmp/payroll_aug_evidence.csv'
FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' OPTIONALLY ENCLOSED BY '"' LINES TERMINATED BY '\n';

```sql
-- PostgreSQL (psql, client-side, works with a read-only account and no server filesystem access)
```
\copy (SELECT employee_id, pay_month, basic_salary, net_pay FROM payroll WHERE pay_month = '2026-08-01') TO 'payroll_aug.csv' CSV HEADER

Most GUI clients offer a one-click "Export result set" that produces the same thing without touching the server's filesystem at all (DBeaver, Workbench, pgAdmin all have this in the results grid's right-click menu or toolbar) — for a tester on a restricted, read-only account, this client-side export is usually the only option and the right default regardless, since it doesn't need any server-side file privilege. Always include a header row (FIELDS/HEADER above) so the reader doesn't have to guess which column is which by position.
## Formatted text for chat and tickets
For a quick Slack message or a short evidence block inside a ticket description, a manually-formatted (or client-generated) text table is often more readable inline than an attached file, especially for small result sets — exactly the |-delimited tables used throughout this manual:
employee_id | pay_month  | copies
2           | 2026-08-01 | 2

Most clients can generate this directly (DBeaver: right-click a result → "Advanced Copy" → various text formats including Markdown tables), which is faster and less error-prone than typing it by hand.
## Always include the query itself
Whatever export format, paste the exact SQL alongside it — as a code block in the ticket, or as a comment header in the CSV/script file. This is non-negotiable evidence, for three reasons that echo points made throughout Parts 6 and 10: it lets the developer re-run the query themselves to confirm the fix later (closing the loop 10.2's baselines describe); it lets a reviewer spot a mistake in the query itself (an unintended LEFT JOIN fan-out, 4.1, that inflated a count) rather than chasing a phantom application bug; and it documents exactly which filters and assumptions were in play (which environment, which date range, which status values were included), all of which earlier chapters (6.1's "which rules were applied," 10.2's check headers) have insisted on capturing.
## JSON export for structured/nested evidence
When the evidence needs to show a hierarchical shape (an API response body alongside the row that produced it, 9.1's comparison pattern) or will be consumed by another tool (attached to an automated test failure, as in 9.4's testInfo.attach example), JSON is often more appropriate than a flat CSV:
```sql
-- MySQL: build a JSON array directly in SQL
SELECT JSON_ARRAYAGG(JSON_OBJECT(
```
| 'leave_request_id', leave_request_id, 'employee_id', employee_id, | 'status', status, 'days', days |
|---|---|
| )) AS evidence | FROM leave_requests WHERE status = 'approved' AND approved_by IS NULL; |

Or, more commonly, format the result as JSON in whichever scripting language ran the query (Python's json.dumps(cursor.fetchall(), default=str), handling Decimal and datetime serialization, which is exactly the string-conversion issue 3.1 and 6.2 already flagged for those types when comparing values — the same care applies when serializing them for a report).
## Redacting sensitive data before it leaves the database
Before attaching any export to a bug report, screenshot, or chat message, check it against 7.6's PII rules — a query result is exactly the kind of place real customer names, emails, salaries or national IDs leak into tools (ticket trackers, chat history) that were never meant to hold them. If the evidence must show real values to make the bug reproducible, either mask the sensitive columns in the export query itself (the same substitution/generalisation techniques from 7.6, applied ad hoc: CONCAT('Employee ', employee_id) instead of the real name) or restrict the evidence to non-sensitive columns plus IDs, and let the developer re-run the query themselves against the real environment where access is already controlled, rather than copying real PII into a less-controlled tool.
## Screenshots: when they're the right choice, and how to make them useful
A screenshot is appropriate when the visual rendering itself is the bug (a UI table showing the wrong value, a chart with a missing bar, 9.6) — in that case, a companion query result showing the correct expected value belongs alongside the screenshot, not instead of it, so the reader can see both "what appeared" and "what should have appeared" together. A screenshot of a raw SQL client result grid, on the other hand, is almost always worse than a proper export: it can't be re-parsed, may be cropped, and often has the query itself scrolled out of view. If a screenshot of a grid feels like the fastest option in the moment, take thirty extra seconds to export the same result as CSV or a formatted table instead — the time saved on the reader's end more than pays it back.
## Packaging a full investigation (the format Parts 4, 6 and 10 have been building toward)
For a substantial finding — an integrity violation from 4.3's scoreboard, a migration defect from 6.1, an anomaly from 10.1 — a single query result is rarely the whole story. The complete package that those chapters have consistently pointed toward looks like:
Summary: one or two sentences, in plain language, of what's wrong.
The query that finds it (with a comment noting which environment and date/time it was run).
The result, exported in full (not truncated), or a representative sample plus a total count if the full result is very large.
Severity and impact: what this affects downstream (money, an audit trail, a user-facing count) — 6.1's severity table and 10.2's severity grading are the template.
A hypothesis about the cause, stated as a hypothesis, not a claim (6.1's "root cause candidates," 8.5's escalation template both modeled this).
What "fixed" looks like: the same query, re-run, returning zero rows (or the accepted baseline count from 10.2) — so there's no ambiguity about what closing the ticket requires.
This is exactly the shape used, in miniature, throughout the worked examples in Parts 4, 6, 8 and 10 — this chapter just names it explicitly as the reusable template it's always implicitly been.
